Neonatal Arctic foxes (Vulpes lagopus) emerge after a gestation period of 52 days [tg = 52 days] at the species' core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], a relatively compressed interval compared to other canids of similar size. At parturition, the altricial neonate weighs a mere 70 grams [Wwb = 70 grams], a value reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by the harsh arctic environment on foetal development. This modest birth mass is approximately one-fiftieth of the adult female body mass, indicative of the substantial postnatal growth required before the young can achieve independence. The newborn pups, typically born in a well-insulated den, are blind and sparsely furred, relying entirely on maternal warmth and milk for thermoregulation and nourishment during the first weeks of life. Field studies in the Canadian high arctic have consistently recorded this neonatal size across various populations, confirming its stability as a life-history trait despite considerable variation in prey availability between years.

As the suckling juvenile grows, it undergoes a series of developmental transitions, with the most critical being the shift from complete maternal dependence to the onset of solid food consumption. Under the same internal thermal conditions that govern all metabolic processes in this species (38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]), weaning—defined as the cessation of milk provisioning by the mother—occurs at 51 days after birth [tx = 51 days after birth]. This timing coincides with the season of peak lemming abundance in many regions, ensuring that newly independent pups encounter a plentiful food supply as they begin to explore beyond the den. The transition to solid food is gradual, with adults initially delivering partially consumed prey to the den entrance before the young begin to hunt small invertebrates and rodents on their own. The relatively early weaning age compared to temperate-zone foxes suggests an evolutionary adaptation to the brief arctic summer, during which pups must accumulate sufficient body reserves to survive their first winter.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs considerably later than the achievement of nutritional independence. At a stable core temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], puberty is attained at 304 days since birth [tp = 304 days since birth]. This means that most individuals born in the spring of one year do not reach reproductive maturity until the following spring, effectively delaying their first breeding opportunity until their second calendar year of life. The delay is energetically strategic: young foxes must allocate resources toward completing skeletal growth and building fat reserves before investing in the demanding processes of reproduction, which include gestation, lactation, and territory defense. During their first winter, sub-adult animals often disperse considerable distances—sometimes exceeding 100 kilometers—to establish territories in areas of suitable habitat. The age at puberty shows some plasticity, with individuals from food-rich years occasionally maturing slightly earlier, but the typical value remains robust across most monitored populations in Greenland and Siberia.

Females produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year] with an average litter size of approximately 9 pups [N_R_i = litter size of approximately 9 pups] under favorable conditions, yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate of 9 pups per year [Ri = 9 pups per year] when food is abundant. In low lemming years, however, litter size may drop to as few as 2 or 3 pups, and some females forgo reproduction entirely—a classic example of reproductive flexibility in a resource-pulse environment. The species' life history strategy is thus one of high fecundity in good years compensated by reproductive restraint in poor years, a pattern that buffers population numbers against the unpredictable arctic food base.

Longevity records for this species show considerable variation between wild and captive conditions. In the wild, few individuals live beyond 4 to 6 years due to intense predation pressure from larger carnivores, starvation during lemming crashes, and the energetic costs of reproduction. However, captive individuals maintained in zoological settings have been documented to survive for as long as approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years], with some exceptional records approaching the upper end of the reported range at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. Such a maximum lifespan of approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] aligns with expectations given the species' internal temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. The ultimate body mass is dimorphic, with adult females reaching approximately 3030 grams [Wwi = approximately 3030 grams] and adult males attaining roughly 3600 grams [Wwi = roughly 3600 grams], a difference likely related to the male's role in territory defense and the energetic demands of lactation on females. Comparative studies with other arctic carnivores reveal that the Arctic fox occupies an intermediate position on the fast-slow continuum of life-history strategies, balancing relatively rapid development and high reproductive output against a moderately extended lifespan.
